terms.gloss: afford, have the money to pay; literally, have something to give
terms.grammar: phrase: habēre with a relative clause in the subjunctive
evidence: Plaut. Trin. 564: vērum quod det nōn habet, but he can’t afford it
Plaut. Asin. 242: sī nōn est quod dēs, if you can’t pay
terms.comment: Latin says what one has to give: nōn habeō quod dem, I can’t afford it; or with est, mihi nōn est quod dem (Plaut. Trin. 761). What one can afford is one’s facultātēs, one’s means (see resources): each gave prō facultāte, as he could afford (Suet. Aug. 57.2).

terms.gloss: be able to pay (what is owed)
terms.grammar: phrase: gerund in the dative with esse
evidence: Cic. Fam. 3.8.2: cum solvendō cīvitātēs nōn essent, when the towns could not afford to pay
Cic. Att. 13.10.3: solvendō enim nōn erat, for he could not pay his debts
terms.comment: Of debts and bills; nōn esse solvendō, to be unable to pay, insolvent.

phrases.latin: Quid cēnsēs? homōst: volt fierī līber, vērum quod det nōn habet.
phrases.english: What do you think? He’s only human: he wants to be freed, but he hasn’t the money to pay for it.

phrases.latin: multārum cīvitātum prīncipēs ad mē dētulērunt sūmptūs dēcernī lēgātīs nimis magnōs, cum solvendō cīvitātēs nōn essent
phrases.english: the leading men of many towns told me that far too much was being voted for the envoys’ expenses, when the towns could not afford to pay

sources: Lewis & Short: habeo · Lewis & Short: solvo
